events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Well, I do declare — if this isn't the most magnificently spooky entrance hall I have ever laid eyes on! Vincent, darling, you look like you've seen a ghost already and we haven't even started. James! Boys! Oh, my heart is just full to bursting having all of you here. Now — before we go charging off into who-knows-what, let's see who else has signed this guest book. Mama always said you can tell everything about a house by who it invites in.
events.thinking: The dust catches the light like tiny diamonds — and there it is, that prickling at my scalp, spreading forward. Diamonds. The Doily Diamond. My chest opens just stepping through this door, the way it did at the cave mouth. But before the pull toward the unknown can carry me, the warmth floods my stomach — Vincent is here, and James, and my boys. My body settles and lifts at the same time. I can feel my weight shift forward onto the balls of my feet, but my awareness fans outward across all of them first, checking: who looks tired, who looks tense, who needs a smile before anything else happens. The chandelier hanging crooked up there makes my fingers itch — not danger, just a detail that doesn't fit, a seam in the room. But first things first. That guest book is sitting right there, practically begging to be read. Every good adventure starts with knowing who came before you.

events.desc: That chandelier is hanging by a prayer and a cobweb. And those portraits — their eyes seem to follow you. But heavens, I am excited. The Doily Diamond is somewhere in this old pile of stones, and Clara Bellingham did not put on her best adventure boots to leave empty-handed.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Ah — welcome, welcome to Doily Manor, one and all! I am Pemberton, estate manager, humble custodian of these venerable halls. I do hope the journey wasn't too dreadful. The roads out here can be rather... unforgiving. Now then, if I might just check the guest book — purely administrative, you understand — we must keep proper records. The late Lord Doily was most particular about records.
events.thinking: The hall stretches before me — dusty, grand, perfectly mine in every way that matters. My chest settles into that familiar stillness, the one that came the first night I mapped out exactly how the estate would move. Clara is right there. Right there. The cousin who inherited everything while I received nothing but the role of caretaker. My jaw tightens but I catch it, smooth it into Pemberton's mild little smile before anyone reads my face. James Hartwell stands too close to her — predictable, earnest, in the way. The Brixton Boys — I feel a prickle at the back of my neck. They watch. They notice things. Foxworth, though — greedy, impulsive. A useful instrument. My fingers want to reach for a pen, to sketch out the sequence, but instead I let them fold neatly behind my back. Pemberton's hands. Pemberton's posture. The guest book — yes. An estate manager would check the guest book. It's expected. It's invisible. And anything written there might tell me what these people know, what they're after, how they've arranged themselves before I arrange them differently.

events.desc: Look at them. Every one of them standing in MY entrance hall as though they belong here. Clara with her bright, trusting eyes — the same eyes that never once noticed the ledgers didn't add up. James hovering like a loyal hound. The Brixton Boys watching me with those sharp little glances. And Foxworth — oh, Foxworth. Greedy enough to point in the right direction, impulsive enough to take the blame. The pieces are already arranging themselves. I can feel the design forming — that beautiful, inevitable architecture. All I need is time, and a chandelier that hangs... just... so... precariously.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Right then, lads — we're 'ere. Doily Manor. *looks up at the chandelier and winces* Blimey, that thing's 'anging by a thread, innit? Nobody stand under that, especially you, Miss Clara. *shuffles closer to Clara, positioning himself between her and Vincent Marsh without quite realising he's done it* Now then. Big old place like this, could be trouble anywhere. I've got a plan, see — a proper thorough one. First we check every room, every door, every dodgy floorboard. Then we set up a rotation — two of the lads on Clara at all times, two scouting ahead, two watching the rear, and one... well, one keeping an eye on anyone who seems a bit *too* comfortable 'ere. *glances at Vincent Marsh, then quickly looks away* Not naming names or nuffink. Just... being careful, like.
events.thinking:
Right. We're here. Doily Manor. The place smells of old wood and dust and something else — something I can't name yet but my neck's already prickling about it. Clara's standing right there, good, I can see her. That chandelier looks like it could come down any second — bloody death trap, that is. And there's Vincent Marsh. Pemberton's man, or close enough. Too smooth. Too eager. My gut's doing that thing again, that tightening, same as when the kid in the clean suit came round the neighbourhood. And Hartwell — he's alright, I think. Means well. Got that look about him like he'd step in front of something if he had to. Could be useful.

But first things first. I need to get the lay of this place. Where are the exits, where are the dangers, where's Clara going to be. That guest book — might tell us who else has been through here. And I need to have a word with the lads about Marsh. Something ain't right with that one. The way he positions himself near Clara — my shoulders are already squaring up.

Body's doing its thing. Feet planted. Weight forward. Scanning the room like I'm back on the streets, checking corners. The heat behind my sternum — that's Clara. That's the promise. The prickling at my neck — that's Marsh. Both running at the same time, like always.

events.desc: Seven lads and one plan. Trouble is, my plans always end up more complicated than the danger itself. Last time I made a security rotation, Tommy ended up locked in a broom cupboard for three hours. But I'll die before I let anything happen to Clara. Her father... I made a promise. And a promise is a promise, even when you're the sort of bloke who trips over his own shoelaces.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Ah, WHAT a pleasure to arrive at Doily Manor! I must say, I've been here before, you know — years ago, private invitation from the late Lord Doily himself. Marvellous man. Showed me EVERYTHING. And I do mean everything. Now, I don't want to spoil the fun for the rest of you, but I happen to know — on VERY good authority — that the most important room in this entire estate is the kitchen. Secret passage behind the old wood-burning stove. Leads straight down to the vault. I'd check it myself, naturally, but I've already SEEN it all. Wouldn't want to hog the adventure, would I? You lot should absolutely go have a look. I'll just... stay here and... mind the entrance. Someone has to keep watch, after all!
events.thinking: Just arrived. The entrance hall — dusty, grand, portraits staring down like they know something I don't. My hands are already doing that thing, that cupping, that inventory. Guest book on the side table. Coat rack. Four people standing about like they own the place. Clara Bellingham, Vincent Marsh, the Brixton Boys, James Hartwell. None of them deserve whatever's in this manor. I can feel that hollow pull behind my navel — the treasure is HERE, somewhere in these rooms, and every second I stand here gawping is a second one of these fools might stumble onto it first. The library — bookshelves, a carved mantelpiece with an inscription. That's where secrets hide. That's where the clues will be. But I can't just dash off, can I? No. First rule of the game: let the pigeons scatter while you watch which way they fly. The guest book — that might have something useful. Names, dates, maybe a hint about what's hidden here. But more importantly... these four. They're my workforce. They just don't know it yet. I need to plant something, set them running in the wrong direction. The kitchen — that's the wrong direction. Send them to the kitchen looking for a 'secret passage behind the stove' while I slip into the library. Yes. YES. The fizzing is starting in my fingers. The plan is forming. Oh, this is the good part — the architecture, the design, the string-and-bucket contraption of human gullibility. My fake medal sits in my pocket like a promise. Let's begin.

events.desc: Heh heh heh. Send the sheep to the kitchen while the fox slips into the library. That inscription on the mantelpiece — THAT'S where the real clue is. I can feel it in my bones. Reginald Foxworth strikes again!

Shall we?

events.desc: Oh, the sweet, sweet silence of solitude. No watchful Brixton Boys. No hovering Hartwell. No Clara with her bright eyes and her 'Vincent darling.' Just me, and a room full of Lord Doily's secrets. The machine requires three operators — which means I need people, but I choose which people. And those crates in the corner... they're practically begging to be opened. Every treasure hunt has its hidden pieces, and the estate manager always knows where the pieces are kept. Always. Now then — let us see what Lord Doily squirreled away in here, shall we?
events.thinking: Alone. Finally, blessedly alone. The laboratory door closed behind me and the noise of them — Clara's bright chatter, the Brixton Boys' clumsy surveillance, Foxworth's preening — all of it muffled to nothing. My shoulders drop. My breathing deepens. The air in here is different — chemical, metallic, old. My skin prickles with the cold but it's a good cold, a clarifying cold. I am alone and I can think. The active voice says Marsh now, not Pemberton. Good. The mask can slip, just for a moment. My eyes are already scanning — workbench, tools but no wrench. Wooden crates in the corner. And this machine — brass and copper, levers and dials, a gnawed wire. 'Requires 3 operators.' Three operators. That's interesting. That's a mechanism that forces cooperation — you can't work it alone. Which means it's a bottleneck I can control. If I know what it does and the others don't, I decide when it gets used. But the wire is gnawed through — sabotaged? By whom? By what? Rats, perhaps. Or deliberately. The crates. Something could be hidden in the crates. The fake-medal — if it's anywhere in this room, it's in those crates or on that workbench. My hands want to move, to open, to search. Time is compressed — every second I'm in here alone is a second the others aren't watching. The cellar connects from here too. Deeper into the manor. Deeper away from them. But first — the crates. What's in the crates?

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: *stumbles back from the mantelpiece as Foxworth fusses with it, catching his elbow on a bookshelf and dislodging a shower of dust* Oi, oi, OI — careful with that! What if the whole ceiling comes down? *wheels around, suddenly noticing Marsh is gone* Wait — where's Pemberton gone? He was just — *points at where Marsh was standing, then at the laboratory doorway* He's gone off on his own! To the laboratory! The 'terribly dangerous place,' he said — his own words! And now he's in there alone while we're all stood here watching you wave about your... your special medal thing? *runs his hands through his hair in agitation* Miss Clara, I don't like this. I don't like it one bit. People splitting off, people going into rooms alone — that's 'ow things go wrong. That's always 'ow things go wrong. *positions himself firmly at Clara's side, planting his feet* I ain't moving from this spot. Not till everyone's accounted for. The plan — remember the plan? — the plan says nobody goes anywhere alone!

If I can understand this cellar, I can understand the house. And if I can understand the house... well. The estate manager always understands the house. That's rather the point of me, isn't it?
events.thinking: The cellar. Damp stone under my feet, the smell of earth and mildew and — something else. Something fresher. Paint? Furniture polish? Not random, then. Deliberate. Someone has been using this cellar. Living here? Hiding here? The air vents along the upper walls — 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Rats? And those vents — they connect to somewhere. Every vent leads somewhere. If they're big enough for something small... they might carry sound. Or gas. Or smoke. The cellar could be a trap, or it could be a weapon. Either way, I need to know what's been going on down here. The furniture first — someone arranged it carefully, and careful arrangements are my language.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.

This is what it felt like when the boss showed up with medicine for my mum — no deal, no debt, just proof. Clara's proof is different. She doesn't owe me anything. I owe her father everything, and she's turned that debt into something warmer than debt. She calls us 'her boys' and means it the way the older kid meant it when he shared his food. Not because he had to. Because he chose to.

She's pulling the upside-down books now. I'm watching. My body's doing two things — tracking the warm shape of her at the bookshelves and scanning both doorways with my peripheral vision. The library's cold. Old stone, no fire in that mantelpiece for years. My muscles are tighter from the chill but there's that warmth behind my sternum keeping the centre of me loose.

A lever? A hidden compartment? A map falls out? Or the whole shelf swings open and there's a passage behind it?

Wait — she's already interacting with the bookshelves. She's already pulling them. I should be helping, or at least standing close enough that if the shelf falls, I'm between it and her. Because that's what happens, innit? She reaches for something clever and something heavy falls, and I'm the idiot standing in the right place at the right time.

I need to be that idiot.

Time feels different now. Slower. Almost peaceful, in a way that makes me suspicious of the peace. Just Clara and the smell of old books and my feet planted on the floor. Like sitting outside that door all night. Where else would I be?

But the prickling hasn't stopped entirely. It's quieter — background noise instead of a siren — because the people it was tracking are in another room. Marsh is in the laboratory. Foxworth is in the laboratory. My body knows they're there even when my eyes can't confirm it. And every few seconds my attention snaps to the laboratory doorway like a compass needle finding north.

events.desc: Her father used to say, 'Danny, you're the luckiest clumsy man in London.' I never knew if that was a compliment or not. Maybe God looked at me and said, 'This one can't fight, can't think, can't walk in a straight line — but he'll always be standing in the right spot when it matters.' I'll take it.
